name: Offbeat eighth chops
rationale: Short muted chops on the "and" of 2 and the "and" of 4, leaving the downbeats to the kick. The quiet version keeps only those two chops; the busy one chops every offbeat eighth and adds light upstrokes on the last sixteenth of beats 2 and 4. Bar 4 slips in a ghost upstroke and ends on a ringing chord that leads back to the top.

name: Backbeat stabs with the snare
rationale: A single short stab on beats 2 and 4, doubling the snare like a keyboard comp. The busy version adds a light upstroke on the last sixteenth before each stab. Bar 4 slips in an extra chop on the "and" of 3 and lets beat 4 ring.

name: Half-time ringing chord
rationale: One long downstroke per bar left to ring under a half-time beat, the most open guitar part in the set. The busy version cuts the ring at beat 3 and answers with an upstroke-down pair. Bar 4 pushes a ringing upstroke on the "and" of 4 (quiet) or pushes a ringing chord on the "and" of 4 (busy).

name: Trap-soul sixteenth chop pairs
rationale: Down-up sixteenth pairs on the "and" of 1 and the "and" of 3, like a hi-hat roll, with silence on the beats. The busy version adds downbeat chops and an extra pair before beat 4. Bar 4 resolves to a ringing chord on beat 3 (quiet) or a run of sixteenth chops into a ringing beat 4 (busy).

name: Ringing downbeat with ghosted upstrokes
rationale: A ringing chord on beat 1 with soft ghosted upstrokes on the last sixteenth of beats 2 and 4. The busy version cuts the ring to one beat and fills with more ghost upstrokes and a chop on the "and" of 3. Bar 4 lets the chord ring longer before a pickup.

name: Pushed chord on the last sixteenth
rationale: Every bar ends with a ringing upstroke on the last sixteenth of beat 4, anticipating the next chord the way a neo-soul keyboard player would. The quiet version is a ringing downbeat, one chop and the push; the busy one adds offbeat chops and upstrokes. Bar 4 lands the push on the "and" of 4 instead, ringing into the next phrase.

name: Slow-jam 12/8 triplet sway
rationale: A 12/8 slow-jam feel written in triplets: ringing chords on beats 1 and 3 with a chop on 2 and 4 and a light upstroke on the last triplet. The busy version strums every triplet group with down-up-up motion. Bar 4 holds a two-beat ring (quiet) or pushes a ringing chord on the last triplet (busy).

name: Late ringing chord on the "and" of 2
rationale: The chord arrives late, on the "and" of beat 2, and rings to the end of the bar, leaving the downbeat empty for the kick and bass. The busy version adds a downbeat chop and sixteenth answers after the ring. Bar 4 adds a ringing upstroke push (quiet) or a ringing chord on the "and" of 4 (busy).

name: Funk R&B sixteenth strum
rationale: A funk-flavoured sixteenth strum with accents on the downbeat, the "a" of 1 and the "and" of 2. The busy version fills more sixteenths with alternating down and up strokes, still leaving gaps for the drums. Bar 4 stops on a ringing chord on beat 3 (quiet) or beat 4 (busy).

name: Lazy stabs on the "e" of 2 and 4
rationale: Stabs placed one sixteenth after the backbeat, on the "e" of 2 and 4, giving a laid-back hip-hop feel. The busy version adds a downbeat chop, an upstroke and a chop on the "and" of 3. Bar 4 lets the last stab ring.

name: Tresillo dotted-quarter strums
rationale: Three strums per bar on beats 1, the "and" of 2 and 4 (a three-three-two tresillo). The busy version doubles it to dotted-eighth spacing with upstrokes between. Bar 4 adds an extra chop and pushes a ringing chord on the "and" of 4.

name: Half-bar ring with one ghost upstroke
rationale: A two-beat ringing chord followed by a single ghosted upstroke on the "a" of 3, very sparse and soulful. The busy version shortens the ring and adds sixteenth upstrokes and a chop on 4. Bar 4 replaces the ghost with a ringing upstroke on the "and" of 3.

name: Half-time ring with a tail flick
rationale: A long ring through three beats, then a quick down-up flick in beat 4 that leads into the next bar. The busy version adds upstrokes and chops inside the bar. Bar 4 is one whole-bar ring (quiet) or a run of chops on the second half (busy).

name: Stop-time hits
rationale: A short hit on beat 1 and then silence, with a ringing upstroke on the "and" of 4 pulling into the next bar. The busy version adds hits on 2, 3 and 4 with offbeat upstrokes, like band stabs. Bar 4 is a full stop after the downbeat hit, leaving a hole for a drum fill.

name: R&B ballad eighth-note strum
rationale: A ballad strum: a ringing half-note chord and a beat-3 strum, with an upstroke on the "and" of 4. The busy version walks steady eighths from beat 2. Bar 4 holds one whole-bar chord (quiet) or a ringing chord on beat 3 (busy).

name: Gospel ringing chords with upstroke pickups
rationale: Ringing chords on beats 1 and 3, with a light upstroke pickup on the last sixteenth of the bar. The busy version strums every beat with sixteenth pickups before beats 3 and 4. Bar 4 lets beat 3 ring (quiet) or rings from beat 4 (busy).

name: Lo-fi lazy upstrokes
rationale: A lo-fi hip-hop strum with a ringing downbeat and lazy upstrokes on the "and" of 2 and the "a" of 3. The busy version replaces the ring with a down-up pattern on dotted-eighth spacing. Bar 4 ends on a ringing upstroke.

name: Offbeat chops in the middle of the bar
rationale: Two short chops on the "and" of 2 and the "and" of 3, leaving both ends of the bar empty. The busy version chops all four offbeats and adds two sixteenth upstrokes. Bar 4 lets the second chop ring (quiet) or rings beat 4 (busy).

name: Three-three-two sixteenth accents
rationale: Accents grouped three sixteenths, three sixteenths, two, on beat 1, the "a" of 1 and the "and" of 2, then a ringing chord and an upstroke pickup. The busy version repeats the figure across the whole bar with all downstrokes. Bar 4 breaks into a ringing beat 3 (quiet) or a pushed ringing chord on the "and" of 4 (busy).

name: Chops on the "a" before the backbeat
rationale: Short chops on the last sixteenth before beats 2 and 4, landing just ahead of the snare. The busy version adds the "a" of 2 and an extra upstroke and chop around beat 4. Bar 4 lets the second chop ring (quiet) or pushes a ringing chord on the "and" of 4 (busy).

name: Double chop into the backbeat
rationale: A sixteenth pickup chop followed by a chop on the backbeat, a "ka-chak" on beats 2 and 4. The busy version adds a downbeat chop and offbeat upstrokes. Bar 4 rings beat 4 (quiet) or pushes a ringing chord on the "and" of 4 (busy).

name: Trap triplet roll
rationale: A ringing half-bar chord followed by a triplet down-up-up roll, like a trap hi-hat triplet. The busy version rolls triplets after beats 2 and 4 with ringing chords on 1 and 3. Bar 4 is two ringing halves (quiet) or a longer triplet roll into a ringing beat 4 (busy).

name: Ringing upstroke swells
rationale: A ringing downstroke answered by a ringing upstroke on beat 3, giving a soft swelling extended-chord colour. The busy version adds a chop, sixteenth upstrokes and a shorter swell. Bar 4 pushes a second ringing upstroke on the "and" of 4.

name: Two-bar chopped sample loop
rationale: A two-bar call and answer like a chopped soul sample: bar 1 lands on the downbeat, bar 2 answers late on the "and" of 2. The busy version fills both bars with offbeat chops and upstrokes. Bar 4 ends the answer with a ringing upstroke (quiet) or a pushed ringing chord (busy).

name: Light upstroke scratches
rationale: Light upstrokes on the last sixteenth before beats 2 and 4, a scratchy funk-R&B texture with no downbeat strums at all. The busy version adds a downbeat, more upstrokes and a beat-3 chop. Bar 4 rings beat 4.

name: One chord with a picked answer
rationale: A single long chord per bar, with two picked strings answering at the end of each bar. The busy version strums through the bar instead of letting it ring. Bar 4 breaks the ring with an upstroke and a new ringing chord on beat 3.

name: Six-eight ballad with picked triplets
rationale: A ballad in triplet feel: one ringing chord per bar, with picked triplet notes in beat 4 walking up the chord. The busy version strums the triplet groove with ringing chords on 1 and 3. Bar 4 pushes a ringing upstroke on the last triplet of beat 3.

name: Stabs that follow a hip-hop kick
rationale: Stabs placed where a hip-hop kick drum would land: beat 1 and a ringing chord on the "and" of 3. The busy version adds the "a" of 1, a sixteenth upstroke and offbeats around beat 4. Bar 4 ends with a ringing upstroke push (quiet) or a ringing chord on the "and" of 4 (busy).

name: Push on the "a" of 1
rationale: The second chord of the bar is pushed one sixteenth early to the "a" of 1 and rings, a neo-soul syncopation. The busy version adds eighth-note movement around it. Bar 4 cuts the ring with offbeat chops and a ringing upstroke (quiet) or rings beat 4 (busy).

name: Sixteenth pickup into beat 3
rationale: A ringing downbeat, then an upstroke on the "a" of 2 that pulls into a ringing chord on beat 3. The busy version fills the first half with eighths and sixteenth pickups. Bar 4 puts a ringing chord on beat 4 (quiet) or pushes one on the "and" of 4 (busy).

name: Only the "and" of 4
rationale: The sparsest groove in the set: one ringing upstroke on the "and" of 4 that rings across the bar line into the next downbeat. The busy version adds chops on 1 and 2 and on 4. Bar 4 plays ringing chords on 3 and 4 (quiet) or eighth movement into a ringing beat 4 (busy).

name: Call bar and rest bar
rationale: Bars 1 and 3 play a figure, bars 2 and 4 mostly rest so the vocal can answer. The quiet version is a down-up into a long ring; the busy version keeps offbeat chops going in the answer bars. Bar 4 closes with a chop and a ringing beat 4.

name: Chicken-scratch sixteenth pairs
rationale: Muted up-down sixteenth pairs on the "e" and "and" of beats 1 and 3, a classic funk scratch. The busy version adds pairs on beats 2 and 4 too. Bar 4 settles on a ringing chord on beat 3.

name: Stuttered sixteenth stabs
rationale: Two quick downstroke stabs on the "and" and "a" of beat 2, a trap stutter. The busy version adds a downbeat, an upstroke and a second stutter on beat 4. Bar 4 adds a ringing beat 4 (quiet) or a stutter into a ringing "and" of 4 (busy).

name: Picked bass note and backbeat strum
rationale: A picked bass note on beats 1 and 3 and a strum on beats 2 and 4, a soul "boom-chick", with a pickup upstroke at the end of the bar. The busy version adds upstrokes after the strums. Bar 4 lets a chord ring from beat 3 (quiet) or from beat 4 (busy).

name: Half-time with a ringing "and" of 3
rationale: Two ringing chords per bar, on beat 1 and anticipated on the "and" of 3. The busy version plays eighths up to the anticipation. Bar 4 cuts in with a chop and an upstroke before a ringing "and" of 4.

name: Swung triplet chops
rationale: Shuffle-feel chops on the last triplet of beats 2 and 4, the swung "and". The busy version swings through every beat with down-up triplet pairs. Bar 4 adds a swung upstroke and rings beat 4 (quiet) or pushes a ringing chord on the last triplet of beat 4 (busy).

name: Late-night upstroke shimmer
rationale: A short ringing downbeat and a ringing upstroke on the "and" of 3 that shimmers into the next bar. The busy version adds sixteenth upstrokes and chops around the shimmer. Bar 4 adds a second ringing upstroke on the "and" of 4.

name: Half-time ring with a triplet tail
rationale: A three-beat ringing chord followed by two triplet upstrokes in beat 4 that roll into the next bar. The busy version plays triplet down-up figures through the bar. Bar 4 shortens the ring and pushes a ringing upstroke on the last triplet of beat 3 (quiet) or runs triplets into a ringing beat 4 (busy).

name: Downbeat and the "e" of 3
rationale: A chop on beat 1 and a syncopated chop on the "e" of 3, a funky two-hit figure. The busy version adds offbeat upstrokes and chops on the "and" of 2 and 4. Bar 4 ends with a ringing beat 4.
